back: The ability to track information across the product life cycle by establishing links between objects.
From a requirement back to the scope features and business goals and objectives that triggered it.
From a requirement forward to design, test components and the final product.
Tracing requirements in both directions, backward and forward.
Keeping product information accurate from approval through implementation, including managing changes.

front: The four traceability and monitoring processes
back: Determine the approach; establish relationships and dependencies; select and approve requirements; manage changes to requirements and other product information.
Defines what is traced, to what detail and where, and how changes are proposed, reviewed, decided and recorded.

front: What decides how much traceability is needed?
back: Regulation, organizational standards, product complexity, the risk of product errors, and whether the traces will be used.
Processes that make sure the product being built conforms to its approved requirements, and that changes are governed.

front: Five uses of relationships and dependencies
back: Confirm business value; manage scope; avoid missing requirements; perform impact analysis; make release decisions.
One requirement is part of a larger, parent requirement.
A requirement cannot be implemented until another one is implemented.
A requirement can be implemented, but its benefit is not realized until another one is implemented.
A grid that links product requirements from their origin to the deliverables that satisfy them.

front: A requirement traces back to no objective
back: It may add no value: possible scope creep. Question it.

front: A requirement has no design or test linked to it
back: It risks being missed in the final product.
A lightweight, temporary traceability matrix: a snapshot used on adaptive projects.
A repository for product information with audit trails, version control, workflow and trace links. It does not make requirements good.
Facilitating discussion with stakeholders to negotiate and confirm which requirements go into an iteration, release or project.
Requirements that are verified and validated, and that those with authority agree the team should build.
The boundary containing all approved requirements for a solution, release or iteration.
The product owner's prioritization of the backlog, or the stories chosen in iteration planning. The definition of ready can stand in for approval.
Facilitates and negotiates. Does not approve.
Lists and weights the forces for and against a change, then compares the totals to see whether there is enough support.
A consensus technique using anonymous rounds of expert input until the group converges.
An appeal to change a requirement or other product information after the requirements have been baselined.
Evaluating a proposed change by how it affects related elements: product information, risks, work, schedule and cost.

front: Four outcomes of a proposed change
back: Approved, deferred, rejected, more information required.
Deferred: recorded with a reason and a future date or release. Rejected: recorded with a reason; it will not be done.
The authorized body, such as a change control board, or the product owner in adaptive work. The analyst recommends.

front: Configuration management system vs version control system
back: CMS: ensures the solution conforms to approved information and records changes. VCS: tracks the revision history of a work product; part of a CMS.
Expected. The request becomes a user story in the backlog, and prioritization decides if and when it is done.
Keeping the backlog ranked by value. In adaptive life cycles it is the technique for managing change.

front: Is the product ready? Using a traceability matrix
back: Every approved requirement traces forward to a test that has passed.

front: Is the product ready? Using a backlog
back: The stories planned for the release are done: each meets its acceptance criteria and the definition of done.

front: Another name for the requirements traceability matrix
back: Traceability matrix, or coverage matrix.
Backbone: the top row of activities or epics, left to right. Walking skeleton: the row beneath, the minimally functional end-to-end set (the MVP).
Assembling the information of value to stakeholders and making it consumable for its purpose: to approve, to confirm coverage, to prioritize or to build.
A general term for any document that contains requirements: business requirements document, functional requirements specification, software requirements specification.
